extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing cartoonists, readers interested in New Yorker cartooning and comic craft
extracted.subtask_description: A feature/interview with Roz Chast that conveys practical and aesthetic criteria for making and submitting cartoons for The New Yorker and similar outlets, plus general creative-practice guidance for humor cartooning. Useful as a craft guide and insider description of editorial process, style, and materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct comic voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Cartoonists should have a distinct comic and aesthetic voice; The New Yorker is known for cartoonists each having different voices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chast: "The most wonderful thing about them is their different voices, which is what the magazine's known for." Examples given (George Booth, Charles Addams, Mary Petty, Gahan Wilson, Sam Gross, etc.) show a range of accepted voices; cultivating a singular, recognizable voice is valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of setting and characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Cartoons should feel specific and grounded — not 'nowhereville' — so readers know where they are and who the characters are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chast: "I don't like cartoons that take place in nowhereville. I like cartoons where I know where they're happening. I have to feel like they're real people." Aim for concrete, recognizable details (places, habits, accents) rather than generic props.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity/personal voice (autobiographical material)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using personal life and autobiography is a valid source of material; authenticity in recounting real incidents is effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chast regularly uses autobiographical comics and stories (e.g., family dog story, pieces about her parents). She collects bits from everyday life and turns them into cartoon material; being true to your own perspective can be funny and resonant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical drawing skill is not the primary criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Orthodox drafting skill is not required; cartoons are judged on voice and idea more than precise drafting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chast: "It wasn't about drawing a horse correctly, because that's not what cartoons are about." Editors may correct small drafting details (e.g., mailbox flag), but imperfect or 'ratty' drawing styles (Lynda Barry, Matt Groening comparisons) can be distinctive assets rather than liabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subversive / nonconformist sensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A subversive or idiosyncratic sensibility — younger/female/less orthodox perspectives — can refresh a magazine's humor voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Profile notes Chast as "the first truly subversive New Yorker cartoonist" whose 'ratty' style and alternative-press affinities gave the magazine a stealthy punk sensibility. Being different from house norms (in perspective or tone) can be an advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of formats is acceptable and encouraged
rubrics_metrics.description: Work can span single-panel gags, four-panel strips, autobiographical comics, long-form journalistic comics, lists, typologies, and other formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chast: she does many formats (single-panel, four-panel strips, long journalistic pieces). The New Yorker has allowed her to explore page-length pieces and different formats; choose the format that fits the idea rather than forcing ideas into one mandated form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generate ideas from real life and jot them down
rubrics_metrics.description: Idea generation should be continuous and derived from everyday observations; keep a simple system for capturing ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chast keeps little pieces of paper in a box rather than a formal notebook and pulls from them when assembling a batch. Sources include things kids say, ads, overheard phrases, annoyances that become funny on reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence with resubmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Resubmit cartoons you believe in multiple times rather than giving up after one rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chast: "I resubmit them, and sometimes I rework them. If I really like a cartoon, I’ll just resubmit it and resubmit it until there are like six rejections on the back." Reworking and persistence are part of the publication pathway.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission process and etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow the magazine's submission routines (drop-off days historically, batch submission) and prepare to present rough sketches in batches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Description of The New Yorker's old system: drop-off day, handing in a brown envelope with ~10–12 rough sketches, waiting room, being seen in order. Chast later faxed batches on Tuesday evenings. Understand the house process (how/when editors see work) and adapt to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial interaction: expect small technical notes and occasional heavy-handed edits
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors may give minimal feedback but sometimes make concrete technical corrections; some editors are more hands-on than others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Lee Lorenz casually corrected a mailbox detail in a rough; others 'muck around' with cartoons. Be ready to accept small changes to improve clarity or accuracy but also be prepared to defend important creative choices (e.g., size).

rubrics_metrics.name: Size and layout issues matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Cartoon size and how it fits the magazine's column grid affects presentation and may be contested by the artist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chast has fought for correct sizing; The New Yorker typically prints cartoons in two columns but occasionally used three; artists may need to negotiate size and layout to preserve the work's intended composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of color — applied selectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Color can enhance longer pieces and visual pleasure but rarely increases funniness in small cartoons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chast: color makes the eye happier but doesn't add to the joke; use color for longer-format pieces (covers, longer narratives) where it contributes to looking and tone, rather than for tiny single-panel gags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable comedic subjects and tropes
rubrics_metrics.description: Dark, 'sick', and taboo subjects (death, grim scenarios) are legitimate comic territory; fairytales and children's-book tropes also work well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chast: she loves fairytales, tombstone gags, 'anything to do with death is funny,' and 'sick' jokes. The New Yorker accommodates humor that makes fun of things you're 'not supposed to make fun of.' Choose subject matter that suits your sensibility and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartoons should reflect their time without being slavishly topical
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective cartoons can be timely but do not have to address current events directly; they should nonetheless reflect the era's sensibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chast: "New Yorker cartoons can be very timely but also not, yet somehow they reflect their time even if they're not addressing the week's events." Aim for work that resonates with contemporary readers without depending on ephemeral news hooks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tools, materials, and technique choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Select tools and materials that suit your process (Rapidographs, pens, mechanical pencils, brushes, Bristol board, watercolors/gouache); left/right-handedness affects tool choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chast lists Rapidographs, other pens, mechanical pencils, brushes, Bristol board for washes, and watercolors/gouache for color—plus practical notes (left-handedness limits use of some nibs). Also mentions craft practices (pysanka egg painting using a kistka) as analog creative training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptability across markets while maintaining core voice
rubrics_metrics.description: You can adapt cartoons stylistically for different outlets but should retain your underlying sensibility; forced changes risk producing parody instead of authentic work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Chast tried making cartoons 'with more of a Playboy kind of feeling' and they became parody. Selling to varied outlets (Village Voice, National Lampoon, Ms.) is possible, but be careful when altering your voice for perceived market tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-form/cartoon journalism requires more writing and different planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Longer pieces (documentary or journalistic cartoons) demand more extended writing, planning, and often color or different presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chast's long magazine pieces (lost luggage, alien abduction conference) were assignments and required substantial writing and format considerations; use longer formats for narratives that need more space to breathe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Career reality: diversify income and projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Relying solely on a single prestigious outlet is often insufficient financially; expect to do other illustration work, books, or projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chast: "I can't make a living only doing New Yorker stuff. Most students probably know they'll have to get another job to support their cartooning." Plan for book projects, illustration assignments, teaching, or other revenue streams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentorship / influences: study varied masters
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning from a wide range of historical and contemporary cartoonists and illustrators strengthens craft and voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chast cites Steig, Steinberg, George Price, George Booth, Jules Feiffer, Edward Gorey, etc. Study diverse influences to develop your sensibility; knowing the field's history helps position your own voice.
